title: Testing Fundamentals
description: Build a solid foundation in software testing concepts. Learn the difference between unit tests and integration tests, understand the test pyramid, and write your first xUnit test in ASP.NET Core using [Fact] and [Theory] attributes.

blocks.text: Testing is the practice of writing code that automatically checks whether your application works correctly. Without tests, every change you make — a bug fix, a new feature, a refactor — carries the risk of silently breaking something else. Tests are your safety net, letting you move fast with confidence.

In .NET, xUnit is the modern, community-supported testing framework. It is the default choice for ASP.NET Core projects and integrates cleanly with the .NET CLI, Visual Studio, and Visual Studio Code. xUnit uses the [Fact] attribute for simple tests and [Theory] for data-driven tests that run with multiple inputs.

The test pyramid is a model for organizing your test suite by speed, cost, and reliability. The base is unit tests — fast, cheap, and numerous. The middle layer is integration tests — slower, more complex, testing how components work together. The top is end-to-end (E2E) tests — slowest, most expensive, testing the entire application from the user's perspective.

A well-balanced test suite has many unit tests, fewer integration tests, and very few E2E tests. This is because unit tests catch most bugs quickly and cheaply. Integration tests catch bugs that unit tests miss — where components interact. E2E tests catch the highest-level user workflow bugs but are so slow that you can only afford a handful.

blocks.title: The Test Pyramid Layers
items: Unit Tests (base): Test individual classes or methods in isolation. Run in milliseconds. Hundreds or thousands in a real project.
Integration Tests (middle): Test how multiple components work together — e.g., a controller with a real database. Run in seconds. Dozens in a real project.
End-to-End Tests (top): Test complete user flows through the UI or API. Run in minutes. A handful of critical-path tests.

blocks.text: A unit test checks a single unit of code — typically a method — in complete isolation. External dependencies like databases, file systems, and web services are replaced with test doubles (mocks, stubs, or fakes). The goal is to verify that a specific piece of logic produces the expected output for a given input, with no surprises from the environment.

blocks.title: Write Tests That Are Independent
blocks.text: Each test should be able to run alone or in any order. Tests that depend on each other or on shared state are brittle and produce confusing failures. Use setup and teardown methods, or constructor initialization, to give each test a clean starting point.

An integration test verifies that two or more components work correctly together. For an ASP.NET Core API, this might mean testing that a controller correctly processes a request and calls the service layer, or that a service correctly saves data to a real database. Integration tests are slower than unit tests but catch bugs that unit tests cannot — bugs that arise from the interaction between components.

xUnit tests are plain C# classes. Each test is a public method marked with the [Fact] attribute. The method name should clearly describe what is being tested and what the expected outcome is. A common naming convention is MethodName_Scenario_ExpectedResult.

blocks.title: First xUnit Test with [Fact]
blocks.content: A minimal unit test using xUnit's [Fact] attribute and FluentAssertions-style assertions.

blocks.text: The [Theory] attribute marks a test that should run multiple times with different input values. You supply the data using [InlineData], [MemberData], or [ClassData] attributes. This lets you test many scenarios with a single test method body, reducing duplication and improving coverage.

blocks.title: Data-Driven Test with [Theory] and [InlineData]
blocks.content: A single test method runs with multiple input pairs, verifying the Add method across a range of values.

blocks.text: The Arrange-Act-Assert pattern is the standard structure for writing clear, readable tests. Arrange sets up the test data and system under test. Act executes the method being tested. Assert verifies the outcome. This three-part structure makes every test self-documenting — anyone reading it can immediately see what is being set up, what is happening, and what is expected.

blocks.title: The AAA Pattern in Practice
items: Arrange: Create instances, set input values, configure mocks — everything the test needs before running
Act: Call the single method or operation being tested — keep this to one line
Assert: Verify the result using Assert.Equal, Assert.True, Assert.Throws, or a fluent assertion library

terms.definition: A test that checks a single method or class in isolation, with all external dependencies replaced by test doubles.
The default .NET testing framework using [Fact] and [Theory] attributes to define test methods.
An xUnit attribute marking a test method that runs once with no parameters.
An xUnit attribute marking a data-driven test that runs multiple times with different inputs from [InlineData] or other data sources.
The three-part structure for writing tests: set up inputs, execute the method, then verify the result.

blocks.title: Lesson Summary: Testing Fundamentals
points: The test pyramid recommends many unit tests, fewer integration tests, and very few E2E tests
xUnit is the standard .NET testing framework, using [Fact] for simple tests and [Theory] for data-driven tests
Unit tests run in milliseconds and check individual methods in isolation
Integration tests verify component interactions but are slower and more complex
The Arrange-Act-Assert pattern gives every test a clear, readable structure
Test method names should describe the scenario and expected outcome for easy debugging
blocks.takeaway: Testing is not about proving your code works — it is about catching regressions before they reach production. Start with unit tests for your core logic, add integration tests for critical workflows, and keep your test suite fast enough that running it feels effortless.

blocks.title: Exercise: Write Unit Tests for a Discount Calculator
blocks.description: Create a test class for a discount calculator service with multiple scenarios using both [Fact] and [Theory].
steps: Create a DiscountCalculator class with a CalculateDiscount method that takes a price and a discount percentage
Create a DiscountCalculatorTests class in a separate test project
Write a [Fact] test that verifies a 10 percent discount on $100 returns $90
Write a [Fact] test that verifies a discount percentage above 100 throws an ArgumentOutOfRangeException
Write a [Theory] test with [InlineData] that tests 0 percent, 10 percent, 50 percent, and 99 percent discounts
Write a [Fact] test that verifies a 0 percent discount returns the original price unchanged
blocks.expectedOutcome: A test class with 6 test methods covering normal cases, edge cases, and error conditions. All tests pass. The [Theory] test runs four times from a single method, and [Fact] tests cover boundary conditions and exceptions.

items.text: I can explain the difference between a unit test and an integration test
items.hint: Unit tests check one piece in isolation. Integration tests check how multiple pieces work together.

items.text: I understand the test pyramid and why it has more unit tests than E2E tests
items.hint: Unit tests are fast and cheap. E2E tests are slow and brittle. Run the fast ones most often.

items.text: I can write a basic xUnit test using the [Fact] attribute
items.hint: Create a public method in a test class, mark it [Fact], use Arrange-Act-Assert.

items.text: I know when to use [Theory] with [InlineData] instead of [Fact]
items.hint: [Theory] is for running the same test logic with multiple different inputs.

items.text: I can describe the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern and why it is useful
items.hint: AAA separates setup, execution, and verification so tests are readable and consistent.
